evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解；甲骨文、金文、簡帛形體；《說文》及廣韻條目
evidence.text: The database analyzes 出 in oracle-bone and bronze forms as 止 (a foot) over 凵, with some oracle-bone forms using 囗. It interprets 凵/囗 as a cave or dwelling and the graph as a foot stepping outside, with the original sense ‘go out’. It cites oracle-bone examples 合集5063 王出 (‘the king goes out’), 合集33006 出日 (‘sunrise’), and 合集7205 勿出兵 (‘do not send out troops’); the first is an attested motion use, while the latter examples show contextual extensions. It also cites bronze inscriptions for going out, paying/issuing cloth, issuing commands, and transmitting commands. These examples support early use in multiple related contexts but do not by themselves establish the chronology of each sense. The entry records two Guangyun fanqie readings, 尺類 and 赤律, in departing and entering tone categories respectively. The source reproduces Shuowen’s ‘進也。象艸木益滋上出達也’, which is an early lexicographic account, not independent confirmation of the graph’s earliest form.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 字頭「出」

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, 漢字字形演變資料庫
evidence.text: The database describes the upper part in oracle-bone and bronze forms as 止, representing a foot, and the lower part as a cave-like shape: together, a person stepping outward. This supports the foot-and-enclosure interpretation independently of the Shuowen plant explanation. The page lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript and small-seal categories; its bronze examples include inscription 集成05410. The accessible text does not date individual oracle-bone specimens or spell out a full dated sequence of graphic changes.
evidence.title: 漢字「出」：字形演變

evidence.text: This page describes oracle-bone and bronze 出 as 止 plus 凵, and reports an oracle-bone variant with 囗 instead of 凵, understood as an enclosure/dwelling. It proposes that the feet and enclosure later joined graphically, making the seal form less transparent; in clerical and regular scripts the 止 component became distorted toward a form read as 屮. The page indexes examples from oracle-bone inscriptions (including 合集217 and 合集33050), bronze inscriptions including Western Zhou vessels, Warring States texts, the Shuowen seal form, and the Qin Shuihudi manuscript 睡.效60. Its period labels establish source contexts but no exact first-use date; its account is a source’s analysis, not a direct visual inspection in this research.
evidence.title: 汉字「出」字形演变字源

evidence.source: Baley, “Reconstructing Old Chinese *-ts Using Han-Time Material,” Transactions of the Philological Society
evidence.text: The article reports Baxter and Sagart’s Old Chinese reconstructions for the two uses written 出: Middle Chinese tsyhwit ‘go or come out’ corresponds to OC *t-kʰut, and Middle Chinese tsyhwijH ‘bring or take out’ to OC *t-kʰut-s. It explains that the departing-tone reading’s proposed *-ut-s is supported by its graphic/lexical connection with the entering-tone reading in *-ut. This is a phonological and word-family analysis, not evidence for an extra graphic component or a whole-graph loan. The article presents these reconstructions as Baxter–Sagart’s analysis; it does not independently establish every semantic derivation between the two verbs.
evidence.title: Reconstructing Old Chinese *‐ts Using Han‐Time Material

gaps: The accessed sources do not supply a securely dated earliest oracle-bone token; they identify inscription numbers and broad material categories. The first attested graph and the dating of its earliest use therefore remain unestablished here.

The dossier’s sprout-from-container account is traceable to Shuowen’s own explanation, but the inspected paleographic sources instead analyze early forms as foot plus enclosure. The proposed Qin-era distortion explains the later plant reading, but the specific transition is supported here by a secondary collation rather than a primary glyph-by-glyph study.

The entry cites early oracle-bone and bronze contexts for ‘go out’, sunrise, sending troops, paying cloth, and issuing/transmitting commands, but these selected examples do not establish a complete semantic chronology or the precise links among extensions such as ‘produce’, ‘stand’, and ‘send out’.

No sound component is proposed in the paleographic analysis, so component-specific sound comparison is inapplicable. Baxter–Sagart reconstructions concern the spoken verb(s) recorded by 出, not a phonetic subcomponent.

The repository includes Zhengzhang reconstructions (*kʰljuds / *kʰljud) that differ from Baxter–Sagart *t-kʰut / *t-kʰut-s. No primary Zhengzhang source was inspected to assess the rationale or dialect/variant scope of that comparison.

A search result mentions a Proto-Tibeto-Burman comparison, but no source directly establishing its proposed cognacy or sound history was inspected. The dossier’s caution that most Old Chinese reconstructions are phonetically incompatible is not independently verified here.

The Chinese CUHK entry provides cited readings and Guangyun fanqie, but this research did not verify a modern pronunciation reference for Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, Korean, or Vietnamese; the dossier’s modern readings remain repository metadata.
